newsitem.title: USA: Scientology Church complains to U.N. about Germany.
newsitem.headline: Scientology Church complains to U.N. about Germany.

text.p: The Church of Scientology said on Thursday it had filed a complaint with the United Nations against the German government for "flagrant violations" of the human rights of church members.
It said in a statement that the complaint was prompted by the German state of Bavaria's decision "to prohibit Scientologists from holding public sector jobs."

Scientology, founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, gives would-be members personality tests and then offers courses and literature to help them realise what the church sees as their full potential.
Heber Jentzsch, president of the Church of Scientology International, accused Bavarian Interior Minister Guenther Beckstein of "implementing Adolf Hitler's civil service policy in Bavaria."
"Beckstein, with totalitarian arrogance, is reenacting the anti-Jewish law of April 7, 1933, which forbade public sector employment of Jewish people," Jentzsch said.
The Church's complaint to the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva notes that the Bavarian measure contravenes Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political rights.

"Regrettably, the German government continues to ignore these human rights violations, continues to refuse to admit that they even exist and continues to refuse to enter into a dialogue to seek resolution of this problem," the complaint said, according to the statement from the Church's Los Angeles headquarters.
The Bavarian move represented "flagrant violations of its (Germany's) obligations under human rights treaties which it has signed and ratified."
Bavaria said on Tuesday it would require all state employees to fill out a questionnaire detailing their ties to the Church of Scientology.

The state chancellery said applicants for state jobs, including teachers and police officers, would not be hired if they refused to fill out the questionnaire. Those already employed would face disciplinary measures if they declined.
The Bavarian government has been at the forefront of efforts in Germany designed to place limits on Scientologists.
Leaders of Germany's 16 regional states said last week they would consider whether the Church of Scientology should be put under surveillance by the government's anti-extremist watchdog.

The Bavarian decree also requires any private companies awarded state contracts in certain sensitive fields to sign a statement saying they will not use the methods of Scientology founder L. Ron Hubbard.
Bavaria said the measures were designed to "prevent Scientologists from infiltrating public positions."
Scientology says it has around 30,000 German members. The government puts the figure between 10,000 and 20,000.
